idiom_name: net/http admin mux + net/http/pprof + expvar + chan command + signal.NotifyContext
implementation_notes: Go's standard library already ships most of a control bus: importing net/http/pprof registers profiling handlers, expvar publishes application variables as JSON, and runtime.ReadMemStats/NumGoroutine expose the runtime's own statistics, so the monitoring half is an import rather than a subsystem. Control is an in-process channel (chan command) or a handler on a separate admin mux, with signal.NotifyContext turning SIGTERM/SIGINT into context cancellation for shutdown; goroutines derive from that context so cancellation actually stops the component. The classic EIP form - a dedicated control topic through a broker - is only worth it when the fleet already runs a broker and components cannot be addressed over HTTP.
pitfalls: Importing net/http/pprof or expvar registers handlers on http.DefaultServeMux: if the data-path server uses the default mux too, the control surface ends up on the public port - bind the admin mux to loopback or a separate listener.
An unbuffered command channel makes the HTTP handler block as long as the component is busy; use a buffered channel plus a timeout on the reply, and never hold the request goroutine hostage.
Context cancellation only stops goroutines that derive from that context: a worker created with context.Background survives the stop command and keeps consuming messages.

variants.name: Broker control subjects (NATS) with request/reply acknowledgement
variants.idiom_name: NATS subject namespace control.<component>.cmd/.status with msg.Respond acks
variants.implementation_notes: When the deployment already runs NATS, the control bus is a subject namespace rather than an endpoint: the console publishes to control.<component>.cmd, each component subscribes to its own subject, replies through msg.Respond (the broker's inbox carries the correlated answer) and publishes status or heartbeats on control.<component>.status; wildcards let the console fan a command out to control.*.cmd. Subject naming is the addressing model, so scoping a command means choosing a subject, and authorisation is enforced by the broker's account and permission model instead of by the component. Choose this variant when components are ephemeral, behind NAT, or written in several languages - the classic control-bus form pays for itself only with a broker already in the stack.
pitfalls: Core NATS is at-most-once: a command published while a component is restarting is lost silently, so lifecycle commands need request/reply (or JetStream with durable consumers) and a timeout that the console actually reports.
A component subscribed to control.*.cmd executes commands meant for its neighbours; subject ownership must be enforced by broker permissions, not by convention.
Command payloads are untyped bytes: without a schema check in the handler a malformed or hostile message reaches apply() directly.
